newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seen extending panel on Gulf War disease.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seen extending panel on Gulf War disease.

text.p: President Bill Clinton will likely announce on Tuesday a decision to extend a presidential commission investigating illnesses afflicting U.S. troops who fought in the 1991 Gulf War, an administration official said.
The panel submitted its report to Clinton on Dec. 31 and he has been reviewing it while on vacation on the U.S. Virgin Islands. The report is due to be made public on Tuesday.
A U.S. official told Reuters on Friday that members of the panel would be asked to continue their work, although this was not intended as a criticism of the Defence Department.
"I think it will be extended a bit, but it is in no way intended to impugn the integrity of the Pentagon," the official said.

The official, who asked not to be identified, said members of the panel included some Pentagon officials and the committee was working "hand in glove" with military officials investigating widespread complaints by Gulf War veterans of illnesses that many feared were linked to exposure to biological and chemical weapons.
The Pentagon has said it has found no common cause of the illnesses and there is no evidence of U.S. deaths or injuries from chemical agents or Iraqi use of them against U.S. forces.

But it also said in October it was notifying about 20,000 Gulf War veterans that they might have been exposed to chemical weapons when U.S. troops destroyed the Khamisiyah weapons dump in southern Iraq in March 1991.
The Health and Human Services and Veterans Affairs departments have been reviewing the panel's report.
"It's safe to say it merits further inquiry," the official said.

A House of Representatives subcommittee chairman said on Dec. 24 he feared the White House panel had not consulted enough sources outside the government, rendering its report "practically meaningless."

Representative Christopher Shays, a Connecticut Republican whose subcommittee has held hearings on the mysterious illnesses, said he had seen drafts of the report and it relied too much on official sources that found no link between the illnesses and biological or chemical weapons.
